introduction: This fourth Sunday of Lent is called Laetare Sunday, from the first word of the entrance antiphon, rejoice, and rose vestments may be worn. Halfway to Easter, the readings speak of God's mercy that never gives up: he sends prophets to an unfaithful people and brings them home from exile. Jesus tells Nicodemus that God so loved the world that he gave his only Son. Let us rejoice in that love and walk toward the light.

prayerOfTheFaithful.invitation: Brothers and sisters, God is rich in mercy and has loved us with a great love. Let us bring our prayers before him.
intentions: For the Church: that she may proclaim to every person that God so loved the world, and that he came not to condemn but to save. Let us pray to the Lord.
For refugees and all who live far from home: that they may find welcome, safety and hope. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those who feel that their lives are beyond repair: that they may discover that by grace they are saved, and that it is never too late to come to the light. Let us pray to the Lord.
For catechumens on their way to Easter: that the light of Christ may grow in them. Let us pray to the Lord.
For ourselves: that we may come out of whatever darkness we hide in and let God's light show us the truth. Let us pray to the Lord.
prayerOfTheFaithful.conclusion: Merciful Father, you sent your Son not to judge the world but to save it. Fill us with joy as Easter draws near, and help us to live as people of the light. Through Christ our Lord.

reflection.title: Rich in mercy
reflection.body:
The first reading tells a sad story with a surprising ending. The people and their leaders were unfaithful again and again. God kept sending messengers "because he had compassion on his people and on his dwelling place," but they mocked them. Jerusalem fell, the temple burned, and the people went into exile. The psalm remembers that time: "By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down." Yet the story does not end there. God moves the heart of a foreign king, Cyrus, and the exiles are sent home.

Paul tells the same story in a single sentence: "But God, being rich in mercy, for his great love with which he loved us, even when we were dead through our trespasses, made us alive together with Christ." He adds, so that we do not miss it, "by grace you have been saved." It is God's gift, not our achievement. And the gift has a purpose: "For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works."

In the Gospel, Jesus speaks to Nicodemus, who has come to him by night. He says the words that sum up the whole Gospel: "For God so loved the world, that he gave his only born Son." And then: "For God didn't send his Son into the world to judge the world, but that the world should be saved through him."

Judgment, Jesus says, happens when we prefer the dark, when we would rather not be seen as we are. "But he who does the truth comes to the light."

That is why this Sunday is a day of joy. Halfway through Lent, we may feel we have not done much. The Church does not scold us; she points to the cross and says: look how much you are loved. This week, bring one thing you would rather keep hidden into the light, in prayer or in confession, and let God's mercy do the rest.
